analysis.investment_thesis: Aegis operates irreplaceable physical infrastructure — LPG and liquid chemical terminals — in a country where LPG consumption is secularly rising and new terminal capacity takes years to permit and build; that is a real, if narrow, moat. The problem is that ROCE of 13.2% sits below my 15% threshold, finance costs have compounded at 28% annually and reached INR 165 Cr, and total debt on a consolidated basis has ballooned to INR 4,606 Cr — this is becoming a leveraged infrastructure play, not a quality compounder.
key_strengths: Operating income CAGR of 21.9% over 9 years despite commodity revenue volatility — terminal fees/throughput business insulates margins from oil price swings
High promoter holding (58.1%) and consistent OCF generation (5/5 years positive, growing from 146 to 558 Cr) indicate management confidence and earnings quality
Physical terminal network (LPG handling, chemical storage) creates genuine barriers to entry — permits, land, capex and safety regulations deter competition
key_risks: Finance costs compounding at 27.9% CAGR; at INR 165 Cr in FY2025, debt service is consuming a growing share of EBITDA — consolidated debt/EBITDA approaches 3.5x
ROCE of 13.2% fails my 15% minimum; each incremental rupee of capex (INR 945 Cr in FY2025 alone) must earn above cost of capital to justify the expansion
Revenue concentration in LPG/petroleum products means regulatory pricing interventions or fuel-switching trends (EVs reducing LPG demand) pose long-term structural risk
red_flags: Discrepancy between 'Borrowings' (INR 2,439 Cr) and 'Total Debt' (INR 4,606 Cr) in FY2025 — the off-balance-sheet or lease-related exposure needs scrutiny
Other income of INR 208 Cr in FY2025 (nearly 20% of reported net profit base) — inflated headline profitability; core operating returns are thinner than they appear
Free cash flow has been negative in 4 of the last 6 years; the business is in heavy investment mode but return on those investments is unproven at scale
analysis.detailed_analysis: Aegis has built a genuinely useful infrastructure franchise over decades — liquid and gas terminals are not easily replicated, and India's LPG consumption story (urbanization, cooking fuel transition) is real. The operating income growth from INR 185 Cr to INR 1,098 Cr over 9 years is impressive and consistent. At P/E of 32x, the valuation is not insane for a toll-road-like infrastructure business with visible growth. However, Munger's inversion exercise raises a serious concern: what if the capex cycle (INR 945 Cr in FY2025) generates returns below the cost of that debt? With finance costs growing 28% annually and ROCE already at only 13.2%, that scenario is not hypothetical. I'd want to see two to three years of improved ROCE as the new terminals ramp before adding capital here.
